metadata.title: Claude, Is This A Problem.
metadata.subtitle: The Is-This-A-Problem Skill
metadata.topic: IS THIS A PROBLEM · CLAUDE SKILLS FOR LEGAL
metadata.purpose: Answer whether Claude decides 'is this a problem' from its own judgment or from a written specification, using the is-this-a-problem skill's own instruction-set pattern as the concrete case. Lands the carry-out that the skill only checks what its spec defines as a problem — same input, same output, every run, and blind to anything the spec never named.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (the checklist step: matching a situation against written conditions, reliable when covered, silent when not)

beats.narration_text: The obvious guess is that Claude weighs a situation and calls it — is this a problem or not. Wrong branch. It's running a written checklist. So what's actually on that list?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'How does Claude decide if this is a problem?', hesitates on 'decide', corrects to 'check', lands the real question

props.text:
How does Claude decide
if this is a problem?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('decide' -> 'check') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: A Skill isn't a plugin or an API — it's a folder. This one is called is-this-a-problem, and inside it is one file, SKILL.md, written in plain language. That file is the whole program: what to look for, in what order, what to say back. The choice is deliberate — text you can read is text you can audit, no hidden logic sitting where the operator can't see it. Claude reads the file, then follows it.

shot.new_visual_element: A folder opening to reveal one file, SKILL.md, growing into an instruction block

production_viz.label: A folder, then a file
production_viz.mechanic: A folder icon labelled 'is-this-a-problem' opens; inside, one file, 'SKILL.md', slides forward and enlarges into a block of plain-language instruction lines. A small figure glyph labelled 'Claude' reads the block left to right, then a checkmark labelled 'follows it' appears beside the figure.

beats.narration_text: The instructions live in a Steps section — a numbered pipeline Claude runs top to bottom. Read the situation, check it against a list of defined conditions, return the answer. Watch that middle step. It isn't Claude weighing the situation with judgment; it's Claude matching the situation against conditions someone already wrote down. The judgment happened once, when the list was written. Every run after that is a lookup.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — a situation flowing through three linear steps: read, check against conditions, answer

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — read, check, answer
production_viz.mechanic: Three boxes appear left to right, connected by arrows: 'read the situation', 'check against conditions' (this one enlarges and holds, accent border), 'answer'. A situation glyph (a small document icon) travels through all three in sequence, pausing at the middle box while a short list of condition lines fades in beside it. THE ANCHOR. The middle box and its condition list are the composition that returns at B03.

beats.narration_text: Back to that middle box. Feed it a situation the list anticipated, and you get the same answer every time — reliable, on repeat. Feed it something the list never named, and there's nothing to fall back on. Not wrong, exactly — just silent, because the spec never gave that case a name. That's the trade a written checklist makes on purpose: consistency where it applies, silence everywhere else. It works if you value reproducibility. It fails if you need the tool to reach past what was written.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — the same checklist box answering a covered situation the same way three times, then an uncovered situation passing through with no answer

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — reliable, then silent
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 CHECK BOX RETURNS, identical. Three covered-situation glyphs pass through it one after another, each producing the same labelled answer card (teal, 'consistent'). Then a fourth situation glyph, drawn slightly differently (a question-mark texture), passes through the same box; no answer card appears, and a small label reads 'not named — no answer', in terracotta, distinct from a wrong answer.

beats.narration_text: When Claude says 'is this a problem,' it means: is this a problem according to the checklist it was handed. Same input, same output, every run. Blind to anything the checklist never thought to name.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: pick one decision you currently make by gut feel — is this urgent, is this worth escalating, is this actually a problem. Before working any specific case, ask the model to help you write out the actual conditions you're silently checking, as a short numbered checklist in the order you apply them. For each condition, have it name what a covered case looks like and what would fall outside the list entirely. Then run your next three real cases through it, one at a time, and flag anything that doesn't fit. Go deeper: ask the same model to run its gut-feel judgment on those same three cases first, without the checklist, then compare the two answers. The gaps are where your list is incomplete — or where your gut is.

llm_exercise.prompt: I make one decision by gut feel — [name it: 'is this urgent', 'is this worth escalating', 'is this actually a problem']. Before working any specific case, help me write out the actual conditions I'm silently checking, as a short numbered checklist in the order I apply them. For each condition, name what a covered case looks like and what would fall outside the list entirely — the situations the list couldn't answer without guessing. Then walk my next three real cases through it, one at a time, and flag anything that doesn't fit.
